title: Single Number
description:
Given a non-empty array of integers nums, every element appears twice except for one. Find that single one.

You must implement a solution with linear runtime and constant extra space.
constraints: Each element appears twice except for one element which appears once.
hints: What is x XOR x? What is x XOR 0?
XOR all numbers together — pairs cancel out.
explanation: Constant space rules out a hash map. XOR is commutative so order doesn't matter.

editorial.approach: XOR every element. Duplicates cancel (a^a = 0) leaving the unique value.

title: Majority Element
description: Given an array nums of size n, return the majority element — the element that appears more than ⌊n / 2⌋ times. You may assume it always exists.
hints: Sorting puts the majority at index n/2.
Boyer-Moore voting: keep a candidate and a counter.
explanation: More than half means it outlives every other element in a pairwise cancel-out.

editorial.approach: Boyer-Moore voting: when count hits 0 pick the current element as candidate; +1 for equal, -1 otherwise.

title: Missing Number
description: Given an array nums containing n distinct numbers in the range [0, n], return the only number in the range that is missing from the array.
hints: The sum 0 + 1 + … + n is n(n+1)/2.
Subtract the actual sum.
explanation: The range has n+1 values but the array only n, so exactly one is absent.

editorial.approach: Expected sum minus actual sum (or XOR indices with values).

title: Move Zeroes
description: Given an integer array nums, move all 0's to the end while maintaining the relative order of the non-zero elements. Do it in-place and return the modified array.
hints: Keep a write pointer for the next non-zero position.
After copying all non-zeros forward, fill the rest with zeros.
explanation: Relative order of non-zero values must not change, so you can't just sort.

editorial.approach: Two pointers: swap each non-zero element into the write position.

title: Plus One
description: You are given a large integer represented as an array digits, most significant digit first. Increment the integer by one and return the resulting array of digits.
constraints: No leading zeros except the number 0 itself.
hints: Walk from the last digit; a 9 becomes 0 and carries.
If every digit was 9 you need one extra leading 1.
explanation: The number can have 100 digits, so converting to an int would overflow in most languages.

editorial.approach: Simulate carry from the right; return early once a digit < 9 is incremented.

title: Valid Palindrome
description:
A phrase is a palindrome if, after converting all uppercase letters into lowercase and removing all non-alphanumeric characters, it reads the same forward and backward.

Given a string s, return true if it is a palindrome.
constraints: s consists only of printable ASCII characters.
hints: Use two pointers from both ends, skipping non-alphanumeric characters.
Compare characters case-insensitively.
explanation: Only letters and digits count; everything else is ignored.

sampleTests.input: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"

editorial.approach: Filter to lowercase alphanumerics, compare with its reverse (or two pointers for O(1) space).
editorial.complexity: Time O(n) · Space O(1) with two pointers

title: Reverse Integer
description: Given a signed 32-bit integer x, return x with its digits reversed. If reversing causes the value to go outside the signed 32-bit range [-2^31, 2^31 - 1], return 0.
hints: Pop the last digit with x % 10 and push it onto the result.
Before pushing, check whether result * 10 + digit would overflow.
explanation: Assume your environment can't store 64-bit integers; detect overflow before it happens.

editorial.approach: Reverse digits, then verify the result is within 32-bit bounds.

title: Roman to Integer
description: Roman numerals use I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000. A smaller symbol before a larger one is subtracted (e.g. IV = 4, CM = 900). Given a roman numeral, convert it to an integer.
constraints: s is a valid roman numeral in the range [1, 3999].
hints: If a symbol is smaller than the one after it, subtract it; otherwise add it.
edgeCases: Subtractive pairs IV, IX, XL, XC, CD, CM
explanation: Scan left to right comparing each value with the next one.

editorial.approach: Map symbols to values; subtract when the next symbol is larger.

title: Power of Two
description: Given an integer n, return true if it is a power of two. Otherwise, return false.
hints: A power of two has exactly one set bit.
n & (n - 1) clears the lowest set bit.
explanation: Can you solve it without loops or recursion? Bit tricks give O(1).

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
description: Given an array of integers heights representing the histogram's bar heights where each bar's width is 1, return the area of the largest rectangle in the histogram.
hints: For each bar, find how far it can extend left and right while bars are at least as tall.
A monotonic increasing stack finds those boundaries in one pass.
explanation: The rectangle's height is limited by its shortest bar. Every bar is the shortest of some maximal rectangle.

editorial.approach: Monotonic stack of indices; when a shorter bar arrives, pop and compute the area of the popped bar extending to the current index.

title: House Robber
description: You are a robber planning to rob houses along a street. Adjacent houses have connected security systems, so you cannot rob two adjacent houses. Given nums (money in each house), return the maximum amount you can rob.
hints: At each house choose: rob it (plus best up to i-2) or skip it (best up to i-1).
You only need the last two DP values.
edgeCases: Skipping two houses in a row is sometimes optimal like [2,1,1,2]
explanation: dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]).

editorial.approach: Rolling DP with two variables.

title: Coin Change
description: You are given coin denominations coins and a total amount. Return the fewest number of coins needed to make up that amount, or -1 if it cannot be made. You have an infinite number of each coin.
hints: Greedy (largest coin first) fails for some coin systems.
dp[a] = 1 + min(dp[a - c]) over coins c ≤ a.
explanation: Unbounded knapsack minimising count. Build answers for every amount from 0 up.

editorial.approach: Bottom-up DP over amounts.

title: Longest Increasing Subsequence
description: Given an integer array nums, return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
hints: O(n²): dp[i] = 1 + max(dp[j]) for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].
O(n log n): keep tails[k] = smallest tail of an increasing subsequence of length k+1, and binary search.
explanation: A subsequence need not be contiguous, but order must be preserved.

editorial.approach: Patience sorting with binary search on the tails array.
editorial.complexity: Time O(n log n) · Space O(n)

title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
description: An ascending array of unique elements was rotated between 1 and n times. Given the rotated array nums, return its minimum element in O(log n) time.
constraints: All integers of nums are unique.
hints: Compare nums[mid] with nums[right].
If nums[mid] > nums[right], the minimum is to the right of mid.
explanation: The minimum is the rotation point — the only place where order breaks.

editorial.approach: Binary search narrowing toward the rotation point.

title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
description: Given a possibly rotated ascending array nums of distinct values and an integer target, return the index of target or -1 if it is not present. Your algorithm must run in O(log n).
constraints: All values of nums are unique.
hints: At any mid, at least one half [l..mid] or [mid..r] is sorted.
Check whether target lies inside the sorted half; if so search there, else the other half.
explanation: Modified binary search — decide which side is sorted at every step.

editorial.approach: Binary search, choosing the sorted half each iteration.

title: Unique Paths
description: A robot on an m x n grid starts at the top-left corner and can only move down or right. How many unique paths lead to the bottom-right corner?
hints: Paths to a cell = paths from above + paths from the left.
Or count arrangements: choose which (m-1) of the (m+n-2) moves are 'down'.
explanation: Grid DP or the binomial coefficient C(m+n-2, m-1).

editorial.approach: 1-D DP row: row[j] += row[j-1].

title: Decode Ways
description: A message of letters is encoded with 'A' → "1" … 'Z' → "26". Given a string s of digits, return the number of ways to decode it.
constraints: s contains only digits and may contain leading zero(s).
hints: A single digit is decodable if it's 1-9; a pair if it's 10-26.
dp[i] = (dp[i-1] if s[i-1] valid) + (dp[i-2] if s[i-2:i] valid).
explanation: Like climbing stairs, but each step is only allowed when the digits form a valid code.

editorial.approach: Rolling DP with two previous counts.

title: Palindromic Substrings
description: Given a string s, return the number of palindromic substrings in it. Substrings at different positions count separately even if they are equal.
constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters.
hints: Every palindrome has a center — either a character or a gap between two characters.
Expand around each of the 2n-1 centers.
explanation: Count occurrences, not distinct palindromes.

editorial.approach: Expand around centers.

title: Sqrt(x)
description: Given a non-negative integer x, return the square root of x rounded down to the nearest integer. You must not use any built-in exponent function or operator.
hints: Binary search the answer in [0, x].
Careful: mid * mid can overflow 32-bit integers — use long or compare mid with x / mid.
explanation: Find the largest k such that k² ≤ x.

editorial.approach: Binary search on k with k*k <= x.

title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
description: Given an unsorted array of integers nums, return the length of the longest consecutive elements sequence. You must write an algorithm that runs in O(n) time.
hints: Put everything in a hash set.
Only start counting from numbers x where x - 1 is NOT in the set.
explanation: Sorting gives O(n log n); the set trick makes each number part of exactly one scan.

editorial.approach: Hash set; extend sequences only from their starting element.

title: Subarray Sum Equals K
description: Given an array of integers nums and an integer k, return the total number of contiguous subarrays whose sum equals k.
hints: sum(i..j) = prefix[j] - prefix[i-1].
Count how many earlier prefix sums equal currentPrefix - k using a hash map.
edgeCases: Subarray starting at index 0 — seed the map with {0: 1}
explanation: Because values can be negative, two pointers fail; prefix sums + hash map give O(n).

editorial.approach: Running prefix sum with a frequency map.

title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
description: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, return the kth largest element in the array (in sorted order, not the kth distinct element).
hints: Keep a min-heap of size k; its top is the answer.
Quickselect gives average O(n).
explanation: Can you solve it without fully sorting?

editorial.approach: Min-heap of size k.
editorial.complexity: Time O(n log k) · Space O(k)

title: First Missing Positive
description: Given an unsorted integer array nums, return the smallest positive integer that is not present. You must implement an algorithm that runs in O(n) time and uses O(1) auxiliary space.
hints: The answer is always in [1, n + 1].
Place each value v in 1..n at index v-1 by swapping (cyclic sort); then scan for the first mismatch.
edgeCases: Values larger than n are ignored
explanation: Using the array itself as a hash table satisfies the O(1) space requirement.

editorial.approach: Cyclic sort values into their slots, then find the first index i with nums[i] != i + 1.

title: Longest Valid Parentheses
description: Given a string containing just the characters '(' and ')', return the length of the longest valid (well-formed) parentheses substring.
hints: Push indices on a stack, seeded with -1 as a base.
On ')', pop; if the stack becomes empty push the current index as the new base, else the length is i - stack.top.
edgeCases: Nested and adjacent valid parts like "()(())"
explanation: The substring must be contiguous and balanced. The base index marks where the last invalid position was.

editorial.approach: Index stack with a sentinel base.

title: Queens That Can Attack the King
description:
On a 0-indexed 8 x 8 chessboard, there can be multiple black queens and one white king.

You are given a 2D integer array queens where queens[i] = [xQueeni, yQueeni] represents the position of the ith black queen on the chessboard. You are also given an integer array king of length 2 where king = [xKing, yKing] represents the position of the white king.

Return the coordinates of the black queens that can directly attack the king. You may return the answer in any order.

 

Example 1:

Input: queens = [[0,1],[1,0],[4,0],[0,4],[3,3],[2,4]], king = [0,0]
Output: [[0,1],[1,0],[3,3]]
Explanation: The diagram above shows the three queens that can directly attack the king and the three queens that cannot attack the king (i.e., marked with red dashes).

Example 2:

Input: queens = [[0,0],[1,1],[2,2],[3,4],[3,5],[4,4],[4,5]], king = [3,3]
Output: [[2,2],[3,4],[4,4]]
Explanation: The diagram above shows the three queens that can directly attack the king and the three queens that cannot attack the king (i.e., marked with red dashes).

 

Constraints:

  • 1 <= queens.length < 64
  • queens[i].length == king.length == 2
  • 0 <= xQueeni, yQueeni, xKing, yKing < 8
  • All the given positions are unique.

editorial.approach: See LeetCode

hints: Check 8 directions around the King.
Find the nearest queen in each direction.
